The LDO noise density alone does not determine the VCO phase noise; you also need the transfer from the LDO output node to the oscillator phase. The usual small-noise calculation is:

Let

- \(v_{n}(t)\) be the small noise voltage at the VCO supply rail after the LDO, with one-sided voltage noise PSD  
  \[
  S_{V_{DD}}(f)\quad [\mathrm{V^2/Hz}]
  \]
  (if the LDO spec is already the output-noise PSD, \(S_{V_{DD}}=S_{\rm th}\); otherwise include the LDO output/decoupling transfer to the VCO rail),
- \(K_{V_{DD}}\) be the VCO supply-pushing gain
  \[
  K_{V_{DD}}=\frac{\partial f_{\rm osc}}{\partial V_{DD}}\quad [\mathrm{Hz/V}]
  \]
  or, more generally, the small-signal transfer from a sinusoidal \(V_{DD}\) perturbation at offset \(f_m\) to the VCO instantaneous frequency, \(K_{V_{DD}}(f_m)\).

The supply noise frequency-modulates the oscillator:
\[
\delta f(t)=K_{V_{DD}}v_n(t),
\]
so the instantaneous-frequency noise PSD is
\[
S_f(f_m)=|K_{V_{DD}}(f_m)|^2 S_{V_{DD}}(f_m).
\]
Since phase is the integral of frequency,
\[
S_\phi(f_m)=\frac{S_f(f_m)}{f_m^2}
       =\frac{|K_{V_{DD}}(f_m)|^2 S_{V_{DD}}(f_m)}{f_m^2}.
\]
The single-sideband phase noise (relative to carrier) is therefore
\[
\boxed{
\mathcal L(f_m)
=\frac12 S_\phi(f_m)
=\frac{|K_{V_{DD}}(f_m)|^2 S_{V_{DD}}(f_m)}{2f_m^2}
}
\]
for a one-sided PSD. In dBc/Hz,
\[
\mathcal L_{\rm dBc/Hz}(f_m)
=10\log_{10}\!\left[
\frac{|K_{V_{DD}}(f_m)|^2 S_{V_{DD}}(f_m)}{2f_m^2}
\right].
\]
If the LDO thermal noise is white over the offset of interest and \(K_{V_{DD}}\) is approximately constant, set \(S_{V_{DD}}(f_m)=S_{\rm th}\):
\[
\boxed{
\mathcal L(f_m)\approx \frac{K_{V_{DD}}^2 S_{\rm th}}{2f_m^2}
}
\]
so a white thermal noise gives a \(1/f_m^2\) phase-noise contribution. Any LDO flicker noise would give a \(1/f_m^3\) contribution.

For this specific VCO, \(K_{V_{DD}}\) is found from the actual supply-to-frequency conversion, including the varactor bias, capacitor banks, parasitic capacitances, core nonlinearity, etc. A rough small-signal estimate is
\[
K_{V_{DD}}
=-\frac{f_0}{2C_{\rm eff}}\frac{\partial C_{\rm eff}}{\partial V_{DD}},
\]
where \(C_{\rm eff}\) is the effective tank capacitance seen by the differential mode. The varactors are usually the main path: for an ideal varactor biased by approximately \(V_{DD}-V_{cont}\), changing \(V_{DD}\) is equivalent to changing \(V_{cont}\) with opposite sign, so
\[
|K_{V_{DD}}|\approx |K_{VCO}|
=\left|\frac{\partial f_0}{\partial V_{cont}}\right|
\]
when the only relevant path is the varactor and \(V_{cont}\) is ground-referenced. If \(V_{cont}\) also tracks the LDO rail, use the net variation of \(V_{DD}-V_{cont}\), since the two may cancel.

In practice, the most reliable way to get \(K_{V_{DD}}(f_m)\) or the full phase transfer \(H_{\phi,V_{DD}}(f_m)\) is to simulate the oscillator with a small-signal supply excitation: PSS plus PXF/pnoise or a small injected tone at \(V_{DD}\) and measurement of the resulting sidebands. Then
\[
\mathcal L(f_m)=\frac12 |H_{\phi,V_{DD}}(f_m)|^2 S_{V_{DD}}(f_m),
\]
with \(H_{\phi,V_{DD}}\approx K_{V_{DD}}/f_m\) in the quasi-static/low-offset limit. This automatically includes nonlinear varactor effects, common-mode-to-frequency conversion, AM-to-PM conversion, and mismatch.

Finally, the LDO rail noise is normally common-mode at the differential output. In an ideal symmetric differential oscillator with zero supply pushing, the LDO noise produces no differential phase noise. In the real circuit, the nonlinear varactors and other device capacitances give a finite \(K_{V_{DD}}\), so the above expression applies. The total phase noise is the sum of uncorrelated contributions:
\[
\mathcal L_{\rm tot}(f_m)
=
\mathcal L_{\rm intrinsic}(f_m)
+
\mathcal L_{\rm LDO}(f_m)
+\cdots
\]
(using the same one-sided/two-sided PSD convention throughout).

For the free-running VCO shown, the LDO noise at \(V_{\rm out}\) is mostly common-mode on the tank nodes \(X,Y\). It changes the varactor bias approximately as \(V_X-V_{\rm cont}\approx V_{\rm out}-V_{\rm cont}\), and also changes parasitic MOS/junction capacitances. Hence it frequency-modulates the oscillator.

Define the supply pushing coefficient at the operating point as

\[
K_{\rm push}=\frac{\partial f_0}{\partial V_{\rm DD}}
\quad [\mathrm{Hz/V}],
\qquad
K_\omega=\frac{\partial \omega_0}{\partial V_{\rm DD}}
=2\pi K_{\rm push}
\quad [\mathrm{rad/s/V}].
\]

For an LC tank this is approximately

\[
K_{\rm push}
= -\frac{f_0}{2C_{\rm tank}(V_{\rm DD})}
  \frac{\partial C_{\rm tank}}{\partial V_{\rm DD}},
\]

where \(C_{\rm tank}\) includes the varactors and all supply-dependent parasitic capacitances. In practice, the most reliable way to get it is a periodic steady-state simulation while sweeping the supply voltage by a small amount.

Let \(S_{v_{dd}}(f_m)\) be the one-sided noise PSD at the VCO supply, in \(\mathrm{V^2/Hz}\), at offset \(f_m\) from the carrier. If the LDO is ideal-connected directly to the VCO and no filtering is included, then

\[
S_{v_{dd}}(f_m)=S_{th}(f_m).
\]

If the LDO data sheet gives an amplitude noise density \(e_n\) in \(\mathrm{V/\sqrt{Hz}}\), then use \(S_{th}=e_n^2\).

The supply noise produces instantaneous frequency deviation

\[
f_{\rm inst}(t)=f_0+K_{\rm push}\,v_{dd}(t),
\]

and the phase is the integral of the frequency error:

\[
\phi(t)=2\pi K_{\rm push}\int v_{dd}(t)\,dt.
\]

Thus, at offset \(f_m\), with \(S_{v_{dd}}\) one-sided,

\[
S_\phi(f_m)=\left(\frac{K_{\rm push}}{f_m}\right)^2
S_{v_{dd}}(f_m)
\quad [\mathrm{rad^2/Hz}],
\]

and the single-sideband phase-noise spectrum is

\[
\boxed{
\mathcal L_{\rm LDO}(f_m)
=
\frac{1}{2}
\left(\frac{K_{\rm push}}{f_m}\right)^2
S_{v_{dd}}(f_m)
}
\]

where \(\mathcal L\) is a linear power ratio per Hz. In dBc/Hz:

\[
\boxed{
\mathcal L_{\rm LDO,dB}(f_m)
=
10\log_{10}\!\left[
\frac{K_{\rm push}^2\,S_{v_{dd}}(f_m)}
     {2 f_m^2}
\right]
}
\]

Equivalently, using \(K_\omega\) in \(\mathrm{rad/s/V}\),

\[
\mathcal L_{\rm LDO}(f_m)
=
\frac{K_\omega^2}{8\pi^2 f_m^2}
S_{v_{dd}}(f_m)
=
\frac{K_\omega^2}{2(2\pi f_m)^2}
S_{v_{dd}}(f_m).
\]

For pure white thermal LDO noise, \(S_{v_{dd}}\) is roughly constant, so the LDO contribution to phase noise falls as

\[
\mathcal L_{\rm LDO}(f_m)\propto \frac{1}{f_m^2},
\]

i.e. \(-20\,\mathrm{dB/decade}\). If the LDO noise also has a \(1/f\) flicker component, insert the actual frequency-dependent \(S_{v_{dd}}(f_m)\); the flicker part produces a \(1/f_m^3\) contribution.

For a more exact calculation:

- Replace \(S_{th}\) by the noise actually reaching the VCO supply:
  \[
  S_{v_{dd}}(f_m)=|H_{\rm LDO\to VCO}(f_m)|^2 S_{th}(f_m),
  \]
  where \(H\) includes the LDO output impedance, output capacitor, package inductance, on-chip decoupling, etc.
- Use a periodic small-signal noise analysis (PSS + pnoise) or impulse-sensitivity-function analysis to obtain the full voltage-noise-to-phase transfer:
  \[
  S_\phi(f_m)=|H_{\phi,V_{\rm DD}}(f_m)|^2 S_{v_{dd}}(f_m),
  \qquad
  \mathcal L=\frac{1}{2}S_\phi,
  \]
  using a one-sided \(S_\phi\). This automatically includes high-frequency folding and finite tank bandwidth. The simple \(K_{\rm push}\) formula above is the low-frequency/adiabatic approximation and is usually accurate for offsets well below \(f_0\) and below the LDO/decoupling bandwidth.
- If the LDO noise reaches other bias/control nodes, combine the paths coherently before squaring. For example, if \(V_{\rm cont}\) also moves with the LDO,
  \[
  K_{\rm eff}(f_m)
  =
  K_{V_{\rm DD}}H_{V_{\rm DD}}(f_m)
  +
  K_{V_{\rm cont}}H_{V_{\rm cont}}(f_m)+\cdots,
  \]
  then use \(|K_{\rm eff}|^2/f_m^2\) in the phase-noise formula. In the schematic, if \(V_{\rm cont}\) is ground-referenced, LDO noise changes \(V_{\rm DD}-V_{\rm cont}\); if \(V_{\rm cont}\) is generated from the same LDO and tracks \(V_{\rm DD}\), the common-mode effect can be strongly rejected.

Finally, add this contribution to the intrinsic VCO phase noise in linear power, not directly in dB:

\[
\mathcal L_{\rm total}
=
\mathcal L_{\rm VCO,intrinsic}
+
\mathcal L_{\rm LDO}
+\cdots .
\]

The factor of \(1/2\) depends on convention. If a paper defines the phase PSD as two-sided and writes \(\mathcal L=S_\phi\) for positive offsets, the \(1/2\) is absorbed into that definition; with a two-sided supply-noise PSD at positive frequency, the single-sideband result corresponds to \(K_f^2S_{v_{dd}}^{\rm 2-sided}/f_m^2\).

    *   **Understanding the VCO's Frequency Dependence:** The oscillation frequency of an LC oscillator is approximately given by $\omega_0 \approx 1/\sqrt{L C_{eff}}$, where $L$ is the inductance ($L_1$ in this case) and $C_{eff}$ is the effective capacitance of the resonant tank. In this cross-coupled LC oscillator, $C_{eff}$ is determined by the parasitic capacitances of the transistors $M_1$ and $M_2$, and their operating points.
    *   **Impact of $V_{out}$:** The supply voltage $V_{out}$ directly affects the drain voltages of transistors $M_1$ and $M_2$. Since parasitic capacitances (like drain-bulk capacitance $C_{db}$) are voltage-dependent, changes in $V_{out}$ lead to changes in $C_{eff}$ and thus in the oscillation frequency.
    *   **Deriving $K_{V_{out}}$:** To find $K_{V_{out}}$, one typically performs a small-signal analysis of the VCO. A small perturbation $v_{out\_noise}(t)$ applied to the supply voltage $V_{out}$ will cause a frequency deviation $\Delta\omega(t)$. The parameter $K_{V_{out}}$ is the gain of the transfer function from $v_{out\_noise}$ to $\Delta\omega$ at low frequencies. Mathematically, $K_{V_{out}} = \frac{d\omega}{dV_{out}}$. This derivation involves analyzing the voltage-dependent capacitances of the transistors and their relationship to the drain voltages, which are in turn related to $V_{out}$.

3.  **Calculate the Frequency Noise Spectrum:**
    The noise voltage from the LDO, $v_{LDO\_noise}(t)$, causes a frequency deviation in the VCO given by:
    $\Delta\omega_{LDO}(t) = K_{V_{out}} \cdot v_{LDO\_noise}(t)$
    The power spectral density (PSD) of this frequency noise is:
    $S_{\Delta\omega_{LDO}}(f) = |K_{V_{out}}|^2 \cdot S_{LDO}(f) = |K_{V_{out}}|^2 \cdot S_{th}(f)$

4.  **Convert Frequency Noise to Phase Noise Spectrum:**
    The phase noise $\Delta\phi(t)$ is the integral of the frequency deviation $\Delta\omega(t)$. The relationship between the PSD of the frequency noise $S_{\Delta\omega}(f)$ and the PSD of the phase noise $S_{\phi}(f)$ is given by:
    $S_{\phi}(f) = \frac{S_{\Delta\omega}(f)}{(2\pi f)^2}$
    This formula is valid for offset frequencies $f$ away from the carrier frequency.

    Therefore, the phase noise spectrum at the VCO output due to the LDO thermal noise is:
    $$S_{\phi, LDO}(f) = \frac{|K_{V_{out}}|^2 S_{th}(f)}{(2\pi f)^2}$$

**In summary, to compute the VCO output phase noise from the LDO's thermal noise:**

1.  Obtain the noise spectrum of the LDO, $S_{th}(f)$.
2.  Analyze the VCO circuit to determine the frequency tuning gain with respect to the supply voltage, $K_{V_{out}} = \frac{d\omega}{dV_{out}}$. This involves understanding how the supply voltage affects the resonant tank's effective capacitance through the transistors' voltage-dependent parasitic capacitances.
3.  Use the formula $S_{\phi}(f) = \frac{|K_{V_{out}}|^2 S_{th}(f)}{(2\pi f)^2}$ to calculate the phase noise spectrum at a given offset frequency $f$.

Excellent question. This gets to the heart of how noise from power supplies affects oscillator performance. The process of computing the VCO output phase noise from the LDO's thermal noise involves understanding how supply voltage variations modulate the oscillator's frequency.

Here is a step-by-step explanation, from a simplified intuitive model to a more rigorous one.

### 1. The Core Concept: Frequency Modulation

The fundamental principle is that noise on the LDO output voltage (`Vout`) acts as a small, random perturbation to the VCO's supply. This perturbation modulates the instantaneous oscillation frequency of the VCO. An oscillator effectively integrates frequency variations to produce phase variations. This means that frequency noise is converted into phase noise.

### 2. Mechanisms of Frequency Modulation by Supply Noise

The noise on `Vout` can change the oscillation frequency `f_o` through several mechanisms in this specific circuit:

*   **Varactor Modulation (Dominant Effect):** The varactors (`M_v1`, `M_v2`) are MOS transistors used as voltage-variable capacitors. Their capacitance is a function of the voltage across their terminals (gate-to-source and gate-to-drain). The drains of the cross-coupled pair `M1` and `M2` (nodes X and Y) are connected to the varactor sources. The voltage at nodes X and Y swings around an average DC level that is dependent on `Vout`. Noise on `Vout` directly translates to noise on the average voltage at X and Y. This modulates the varactor capacitance, which in turn changes the total tank capacitance and thus the oscillation frequency (`f_o = 1 / (2π√(L*C_tank))`).
*   **Active Device Modulation:** The noise on `Vout` also modulates the drain-to-source voltage (`V_ds`) of the main switching transistors, `M1` and `M2`. This can change their parasitic capacitances (`C_ds`, `C_gd`) and even their transconductance (`g_m`), which can slightly alter the oscillation frequency.
*   **AM-to-PM Conversion:** Supply noise can modulate the amplitude of the oscillation. Due to circuit nonlinearities (like the varactors), a change in amplitude can lead to a change in frequency. This is known as AM-to-PM (Amplitude Modulation to Phase Modulation) conversion.

### 3. Simplified LTI Model (Linear Time-Invariant)

For a first-order approximation, especially for low-frequency noise, we can treat the VCO as a linear system where a small DC change in `Vout` causes a proportional change in `f_o`.

**Step 1: Find the VCO's Supply Sensitivity (K_supply)**

First, we need to determine how sensitive the VCO's frequency is to changes in its supply voltage. This is a key parameter, often denoted as `K_supply` or `K_VCO,supply`.

`K_supply = d(f_o) / d(Vout)` (Units: Hz/V)

This value can be found by simulating the VCO at two slightly different supply voltages and calculating the slope.

**Step 2: Convert Voltage Noise to Frequency Noise**

The LDO's voltage noise, with a power spectral density (PSD) of `S_th(f)` (in V²/Hz), is converted into frequency noise `S_Δf(f)` (in Hz²/Hz) by this sensitivity factor:

`S_Δf(f) = (K_supply)² * S_th(f)`

**Step 3: Convert Frequency Noise to Phase Noise**

An ideal oscillator integrates frequency noise to produce phase noise. In the frequency domain, this integration corresponds to a `1/f²` shaping. The single-sideband (SSB) phase noise `L(Δf)` at an offset frequency `Δf` from the carrier is related to the frequency noise spectrum by:

`L(Δf) = S_Δf(Δf) / (2 * (Δf)²) `

**Final Calculation:**

Combining these steps, we get the formula for the VCO output phase noise due to the LDO noise:

`L(Δf) ≈ ( (K_supply)² * S_th(Δf) ) / ( 2 * (Δf)² )`

This can be rewritten as:

`L(Δf) ≈ (1/2) * (K_supply / Δf)² * S_th(Δf)`

This equation shows that the phase noise contribution from the LDO will have a `1/f²` slope (20 dB/decade), shaped by the LDO's own noise spectrum `S_th(Δf)`.

### 4. Advanced LTV Model (Linear Time-Variant) & The ISF

The simplified model is accurate for low offset frequencies but misses a key phenomenon: **noise folding**. The VCO is a time-variant system because the sensitivity of its nodes to perturbations changes throughout the oscillation cycle. The **Impulse Sensitivity Function (ISF)**, denoted `Γ(x)`, formally describes this time-varying sensitivity.

*   **What it means:** An impulse of noise injected at the supply node at the peak of the waveform might have a very different effect on the phase than one injected at the zero-crossing.
*   **Consequence (Noise Folding):** Because the sensitivity is periodic, high-frequency noise from the LDO (e.g., noise around multiples of the oscillation frequency, `n*f_o`) can be mixed down (or "folded") to low offset frequencies, contributing to the in-band phase noise. This often raises the phase noise floor.

**How to compute using this model:**

This is typically not done by hand. It requires specialized RF circuit simulators (like Cadence SpectreRF or Keysight ADS). The simulation process is as follows:

1.  **Periodic Steady-State (PSS) Analysis:** The simulator first finds the large-signal periodic solution for the VCO (i.e., its steady-state waveform).
2.  **PNoise (Periodic Noise) Analysis:** The simulator then calculates the effect of noise sources. You would model the LDO as a voltage source with the specified noise spectrum `S_th`. The simulator effectively calculates the time-varying transfer function (related to the ISF) from the LDO output to the VCO phase and computes the final output phase noise, automatically including both the direct conversion (`1/f²` part) and the noise folding effects.

### Summary of a Practical Approach

1.  **For a quick estimate:**
    *   Find `K_supply` by running two DC-initialized transient simulations of the VCO with slightly different `Vout` values and measuring the resulting `f_o`.
    *   Obtain the LDO's noise spectrum `S_th(f)` from its datasheet or a separate simulation.
    *   Use the formula: `L(Δf) ≈ (1/2) * (K_supply / Δf)² * S_th(Δf)`.

2.  **For an accurate result:**
    *   In a circuit simulator, place the full VCO circuit.
    *   Model the LDO output as a voltage source with a noise file or function representing its noise spectral density `S_th`.
    *   Run a PSS + PNoise analysis, specifying the LDO noise source as the input and the VCO output phase noise as the output. The simulator will provide a plot of `L(Δf)`.

Excellent question. This is a classic problem in RFIC design, dealing with how noise from a power supply affects the performance of a sensitive analog block like a VCO.

The process of computing the VCO output phase noise due to the LDO's thermal noise involves understanding how supply voltage variations are converted into frequency variations, which then integrate to become phase variations. This phenomenon is often called "supply pushing."

Here is a step-by-step method to compute the VCO output phase noise, starting with a simplified linear model and then mentioning a more advanced one.

### 1. The Core Concept: AM-to-PM Conversion

Noise on the LDO output voltage (`Vout`) is essentially an Amplitude Modulation (AM) of the supply. The VCO circuit is not perfectly immune to these supply variations. The variations cause changes in the VCO's oscillation frequency, which is a form of Frequency Modulation (FM). This FM is then observed as Phase Modulation (PM), or phase noise, at the output.

The key steps are:
1.  Characterize the LDO noise (`S_th`).
2.  Determine the VCO's sensitivity to supply noise (`K_VCO`).
3.  Use these two to calculate the resulting phase noise.

---

### 2. Simplified Linear Time-Invariant (LTI) Model

This model is intuitive and provides a good first-order approximation, especially for noise at low offset frequencies.

#### Step 1: Define the LDO Noise Spectrum (`S_th(f)`)

The problem states that the LDO generates thermal noise with a power spectral density (PSD) of `S_th(f)`. This is the mean-square noise voltage per unit bandwidth, with units of V²/Hz.
*   `S_th(f)` is generally not flat ("white"). It will have a 1/f component at low frequencies, a flatter region, and potentially peaks and rolloff related to the LDO's internal loop bandwidth and output filtering.

#### Step 2: Determine the VCO's Supply Sensitivity (`K_VCO`)

This is the most critical parameter you need to find for this specific VCO circuit. `K_VCO` quantifies how much the VCO's output frequency changes for a given change in its supply voltage. It is also known as the "pushing figure."

*   **Definition:** `K_VCO = d(f_osc) / d(V_out)`
*   **Units:** Hz/V or (rad/s)/V.

**How to find `K_VCO`?**
The most practical way is through simulation:
1.  Set up your VCO circuit in a simulator (like Spectre RF, ADS, etc.).
2.  Run a DC sweep of the supply voltage `V_out` around its nominal operating point.
3.  For each `V_out` value, measure the steady-state oscillation frequency, `f_osc`.
4.  Plot `f_osc` versus `V_out`. The slope of this curve at the nominal `V_out` is your `K_VCO`.

**What causes this sensitivity in the given circuit?**
*   **Varactors (`M_v1`, `M_v2`):** These are MOS varactors whose capacitance depends on the gate-source voltage. In this topology, the voltage across the varactor is related to `V_out`. A change in `V_out` changes the capacitance, which directly changes the tank's resonant frequency (`f_osc ≈ 1 / (2π * sqrt(L*C_total))`). This is often the dominant mechanism.
*   **Active Devices (`M_1`, `M_2`):** Changes in `V_out` affect the drain-source voltage (`V_ds`) of the cross-coupled pair. This can modulate their parasitic capacitances (e.g., `C_gd`, `C_db`), which are part of the total tank capacitance, `C_total`.
*   **Tail Current Source (`I_VCO`):** The tail current source is not ideal and will have a finite output impedance. Noise on `V_out` can couple to the common-source node of M1/M2, modulating the tail current and the oscillation amplitude, which in turn affects the frequency.

#### Step 3: Compute the Output Phase Noise

Once you have the LDO noise spectrum `S_th(f)` and the VCO sensitivity `K_VCO`, you can compute the phase noise.

1.  **Frequency Noise Spectrum (`S_f(f)`):** The supply voltage noise `S_th(f)` is converted to frequency noise `S_f(f)` by the sensitivity `K_VCO`.
    `S_f(f) = (K_VCO)^2 * S_th(f)`  (Units: Hz²/Hz)

2.  **Phase Noise Spectrum (`S_φ(f)`):** Phase is the integral of frequency. In the frequency domain, this integration corresponds to a `1/f²` shaping.
    `S_φ(f) = S_f(f) / f² = (K_VCO)^2 * S_th(f) / f²` (Units: rad²/Hz)
    Here, `f` is the offset frequency from the carrier.

3.  **Single-Sideband (SSB) Phase Noise (`L(f)`):** This is the standard way to represent phase noise. It is defined as the noise power in a 1 Hz bandwidth at an offset `f` from the carrier, divided by the carrier power. For small phase deviations, it is related to `S_φ(f)` by:
    `L(f) = S_φ(f) / 2`

    Therefore, the final formula is:
    **`L(f) = (1/2) * [ (K_VCO)^2 * S_th(f) / f² ]`**

    In decibels (dBc/Hz):
    **`L(f) [dBc/Hz] = 10 * log10 [ (K_VCO^2 * S_th(f)) / (2 * f²) ]`**

    *   **Important:** Ensure your units are consistent. If `K_VCO` is in Hz/V, `S_th(f)` is in V²/Hz, and `f` is in Hz, the formula works directly.

---

### 3. Advanced Linear Time-Variant (LTV) Model (ISF Method)

The simple LTI model assumes the VCO's sensitivity to supply noise is constant. In reality, an oscillator is a time-varying system. The sensitivity depends on *when* during the oscillation cycle the noise impulse arrives. This is captured by the **Impulse Sensitivity Function (ISF)**.

*   The ISF, denoted `Γ(ωt)`, is a periodic function that describes the phase shift resulting from a small charge impulse injected into a specific node at a specific phase `ωt` of the oscillation.
*   For supply noise, we would define a supply ISF, `Γ_supply(ωt)`.
*   The LDO noise `v_n(t)` injects a current `i_n(t)` into the sensitive nodes (e.g., through the varactors).
*   The LTI model's `K_VCO` is effectively proportional to the DC component of the ISF.
*   The LTV model is more accurate because it also accounts for the **down-conversion of noise** from harmonics of the oscillation frequency (`n*f_osc`). The LDO's noise spectrum `S_th(f)` at frequencies near `f_osc`, `2f_osc`, etc., can be mixed down by the time-varying sensitivity of the VCO and contribute to the phase noise at low offset frequencies.

While the full ISF calculation is complex and typically done with specialized simulation tools, the key takeaway is that the simple `K_VCO` model is most accurate for low-frequency supply noise but may underestimate the total phase noise contribution if the LDO has significant noise at harmonics of the VCO frequency.

### Summary

To compute the VCO output phase noise from the LDO's thermal noise `S_th`:

1.  **Find `K_VCO`:** Simulate the VCO and find its frequency sensitivity to supply voltage changes (`d(f_osc) / d(V_out)` in Hz/V).
2.  **Apply the Formula:** Use the LTI model for a straightforward and often sufficient calculation:
    `L(f) = 10 * log10 [ (K_VCO^2 * S_th(f)) / (2 * f²) ]`
    where `f` is the offset frequency from the carrier.

This calculation will give you the contribution of the LDO noise to the total phase noise profile of the VCO, which typically exhibits a `1/f²` slope due to this upconversion mechanism.

If the LDO generates thermal noise, $V_{out}$ will fluctuate. This fluctuation directly modulates the voltage across the varactors, changing their capacitance and, consequently, modulating the oscillation frequency of the VCO.

### 2. Define the Pushing Gain ($K_{push}$)
To compute the phase noise, you first need to know how sensitive the VCO's frequency is to changes in the supply voltage. This is characterized by the **pushing gain** ($K_{push}$), usually expressed in Hz/V:

$$K_{push} = \frac{\partial f_{osc}}{\partial V_{out}}$$

*Note: This value is typically found via circuit simulation (e.g., SPICE) by sweeping the supply voltage and measuring the change in oscillation frequency.*

### 3. Compute the Frequency Noise PSD

$$S_{\Delta f}(f) = K_{push}^2 \cdot S_{th}$$

$$S_{\phi}(f) = \frac{S_{\Delta f}(f)}{f^2} = \frac{K_{push}^2 \cdot S_{th}}{f^2}$$

Here is the step-by-step computation:

### 1. Identify the Coupling Mechanism (VCO Pushing)
In this specific LC VCO topology, the oscillation frequency depends on the capacitance of the varactors ($M_{v1}$ and $M_{v2}$).
*   The DC voltage at nodes X and Y is equal to the supply voltage $V_{out}$ (because the inductors $L_1$ act as DC shorts).
*   The tuning voltage is $V_{cont}$.
*   The voltage across the varactors is $V_{var} = V_{out} - V_{cont}$.

Because the varactor capacitance depends on the voltage across it, any noise on $V_{out}$ will modulate the varactor capacitance, thereby modulating the oscillation frequency. The sensitivity of the VCO frequency to the supply voltage is called the **pushing gain ($K_{push}$)**, typically measured in Hz/V.

### 2. Relate Voltage Noise to Frequency Noise
Let the LDO thermal noise voltage be $v_n(t)$, which has a Power Spectral Density (PSD) of $S_{th}$ (in $V^2/Hz$).
The instantaneous frequency deviation $\Delta f(t)$ caused by this noise is:
$$\Delta f(t) = K_{push} \cdot v_n(t)$$

### 3. Relate Frequency Noise to Phase Noise
Phase is the integral of angular frequency over time. The phase variation $\phi(t)$ is:
$$\phi(t) = 2\pi \int \Delta f(t) dt = 2\pi K_{push} \int v_n(t) dt$$

In the frequency domain, integration corresponds to dividing by $j\omega_m$ (where $\omega_m = 2\pi f_m$, and $f_m$ is the offset frequency from the carrier).
$$\Phi(f_m) = \frac{2\pi K_{push}}{j 2\pi f_m} V_n(f_m) = \frac{K_{push}}{j f_m} V_n(f_m)$$

$$S_\phi(f_m) = \left| \frac{K_{push}}{j f_m} \right|^2 S_{th}$$
$$S_\phi(f_m) = \frac{K_{push}^2}{f_m^2} S_{th} \quad [\text{rad}^2/\text{Hz}]$$

In RF engineering, phase noise is usually expressed as Single-Sideband (SSB) phase noise, denoted as $\mathcal{L}(f_m)$. For small phase deviations, $\mathcal{L}(f_m)$ is half of the double-sided phase noise PSD:
$$\mathcal{L}(f_m) = \frac{1}{2} S_\phi(f_m) = \frac{K_{push}^2}{2 f_m^2} S_{th}$$

Expressed in decibels relative to the carrier per hertz (dBc/Hz):
$$\mathcal{L}(f_m) = 10 \log_{10} \left( \frac{K_{push}^2 \cdot S_{th}}{2 f_m^2} \right) \quad [\text{dBc/Hz}]$$

*   **$S_{th}$**: The given thermal noise PSD of the LDO ($V^2/Hz$).
*   **$K_{push}$**: The supply pushing gain of the VCO (Hz/V), which must be found via simulation or measurement of this specific circuit.

To compute the VCO output phase noise resulting from the thermal noise of the LDO regulator, we must analyze how supply voltage fluctuations modulate the oscillation frequency of the VCO. 

This mechanism is known as **supply pushing**, and it is the dominant path through which low-frequency supply noise is converted into phase noise near the carrier.

Here is the step-by-step method to compute the resulting phase noise.

---

### 1. Define the Supply Pushing Factor ($K_{\text{push}}$)
Any change in the LDO output voltage $V_{\text{out}}$ shifts the common-mode voltage at nodes $X$ and $Y$ (since the inductors $L_1$ have negligible DC resistance). This shifts the bias voltage across the varactors $M_{v1}$ and $M_{v2}$, changing their capacitance and thus shifting the oscillation frequency $f_{\text{osc}}$.

We define the **supply pushing factor** ($K_{\text{push}}$) as:
$$K_{\text{push}} = \frac{\partial f_{\text{osc}}}{\partial V_{\text{out}}} \quad \left[\text{Hz/V}\right]$$

### 2. Relate Supply Noise to Frequency Deviation
Let the LDO output thermal noise voltage spectral density be $S_{\text{LDO}}(f_m) = S_{\text{th}}$ (expressed in $\text{V}^2/\text{Hz}$), where $f_m$ is the offset frequency from the carrier.

This noise voltage modulates the instantaneous frequency of the VCO:
$$\Delta f(t) = K_{\text{push}} \cdot v_n(t)$$

### 3. Convert Frequency Modulation (FM) to Phase Noise
The instantaneous phase deviation $\theta_n(t)$ is the time integral of the frequency deviation:
$$\theta_n(t) = 2\pi \int \Delta f(t) \, dt = 2\pi K_{\text{push}} \int v_n(t) \, dt$$

In the frequency domain, integration corresponds to division by $j 2\pi f_m$. Therefore, the power spectral density (PSD) of the phase deviation, $S_{\theta}(f_m)$ (in $\text{rad}^2/\text{Hz}$), is:
$$S_{\theta}(f_m) = \left| \frac{2\pi K_{\text{push}}}{j 2\pi f_m} \right|^2 S_{\text{LDO}}(f_m) = \frac{K_{\text{push}}^2}{f_m^2} S_{\text{th}}(f_m)$$

### 4. Compute the Single-Sideband (SSB) Phase Noise
The single-sideband phase noise $\mathcal{L}(f_m)$ (usually expressed in $\text{dBc/Hz}$) is half of the phase fluctuation spectral density:

$$\mathcal{L}(f_m) = \frac{1}{2} S_{\theta}(f_m) = \frac{K_{\text{push}}^2}{2 f_m^2} S_{\text{th}}(f_m)$$

In logarithmic terms ($\text{dBc/Hz}$):
$$\mathcal{L}(f_m) = 10 \log_{10} \left( \frac{K_{\text{push}}^2 \cdot S_{\text{th}}(f_m)}{2 f_m^2} \right)$$

---

### How to Determine the Parameters in Practice

1. **Find $S_{\text{th}}(f_m)$:** 
   Run a noise analysis (or periodic noise analysis, $pnoise$) on the LDO regulator alone to find its output voltage noise PSD $S_{\text{LDO}}(f_m)$ at the offset frequency of interest $f_m$.
   
2. **Find $K_{\text{push}}$:**
   * **Via Simulation:** Run a transient or periodic steady-state (PSS) simulation of the VCO. Sweep the DC supply voltage $V_{\text{out}}$ by a small amount (e.g., $\pm 50\text{ mV}$) and measure the resulting oscillation frequency $f_{\text{osc}}$. Plot $f_{\text{osc}}$ vs. $V_{\text{out}}$; the slope of this curve at the nominal operating voltage is $K_{\text{push}}$.
   * **Analytical approximation:** 
     $$K_{\text{push}} \approx \frac{\partial f_{\text{osc}}}{\partial C_{\text{var}}} \cdot \frac{\partial C_{\text{var}}}{\partial V_{\text{out}}}$$
     where $C_{\text{var}}$ is the varactor capacitance.

### Summary of the Final Phase Noise Contribution
The phase noise contribution of the LDO at an offset frequency $f_m$ is:
$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{LDO}}(f_m) = \frac{K_{\text{push}}^2}{2 f_m^2} S_{\text{th}}(f_m)$$

*Note: Because of the $1/f_m^2$ term, any white thermal noise from the LDO ($S_{\text{th}} = \text{constant}$) will manifest as a $-20\text{ dB/dec}$ phase noise slope ($1/f^2$ region). To compute the VCO output phase noise caused by the thermal noise of the LDO regulator, we must analyze how the supply voltage noise converts into phase fluctuations. 

In an LC VCO, the dominant mechanism for this conversion is **supply pushing** (supply-to-frequency conversion). Here is the step-by-step derivation and method to compute the resulting phase noise.

---

### 1. The Physical Mechanism (Supply Pushing)
The LDO output voltage $V_{\text{out}}$ acts as the supply voltage for the LC tank. 
* The common-mode voltage of the oscillating nodes $X$ and $Y$ is directly set by $V_{\text{out}}$ (since the DC voltage drop across the inductors $L_1$ is negligible).
* The varactors $M_{v1}$ and $M_{v2}$ have their gates connected to nodes $X$ and $Y$, and their source/drain/bulk terminals connected to the control voltage $V_{\text{cont}}$.
* Any noise voltage $v_{n,\text{LDO}}(t)$ on $V_{\text{out}}$ modulates the common-mode voltage at $X$ and $Y$. This changes the average gate-to-source voltage ($V_{GS}$) of the varactors, modulating their capacitance $C_{\text{var}}$ and directly shifting the oscillation frequency $f_{\text{osc}}$.

---

### 2. Mathematical Formulation

#### Step 1: Define the Supply Pushing Sensitivity ($K_{\text{push}}$)
The supply pushing factor, $K_{\text{push}}$, quantifies how sensitive the oscillation frequency is to changes in the supply voltage:
$$K_{\text{push}} = \frac{\partial f_{\text{osc}}}{\partial V_{\text{out}}} \quad \left[\text{Hz/V}\right]$$

#### Step 2: Frequency Modulation by LDO Noise
Let the LDO output voltage noise have a single-sided power spectral density (PSD) denoted by $S_{\text{th}}(f)$ (in $\text{V}^2/\text{Hz}$). 

The instantaneous frequency deviation $\Delta f(t)$ due to the LDO noise $v_{n,\text{LDO}}(t)$ is:
$$\Delta f(t) = K_{\text{push}} \cdot v_{n,\text{LDO}}(t)$$

The power spectral density of this frequency fluctuation, $S_{\Delta f}(f)$, is:
$$S_{\Delta f}(f) = K_{\text{push}}^2 \cdot S_{\text{th}}(f) \quad \left[\text{Hz}^2/\text{Hz}\right]$$

#### Step 3: Convert Frequency Noise to Phase Noise
Since phase $\phi(t)$ is the integral of frequency deviation ($\phi(t) = 2\pi \int \Delta f(t) dt$), the relationship between the phase noise spectrum $S_{\phi}(\Delta f)$ and the frequency noise spectrum in the frequency domain is:
$$S_{\phi}(\Delta f) = \frac{S_{\Delta f}(\Delta f)}{\Delta f^2} = \frac{K_{\text{push}}^2}{\Delta f^2} S_{\text{th}}(\Delta f) \quad \left[\text{rad}^2/\text{Hz}\right]$$
where $\Delta f$ is the offset frequency from the carrier.

The single-sideband (SSB) phase noise $\mathcal{L}(\Delta f)$ (expressed in $\text{dBc/Hz}$) is defined as half of the phase fluctuation spectral density:
$$\mathcal{L}(\Delta f) = \frac{1}{2} S_{\phi}(\Delta f) = \frac{K_{\text{push}}^2}{2 \Delta f^2} S_{\text{th}}(\Delta f)$$

In logarithmic units ($\text{dBc/Hz}$):
$$\mathcal{L}(\Delta f)\Big|_{\text{dBc/Hz}} = 10 \log_{10} \left( \frac{K_{\text{push}}^2 \cdot S_{\text{th}}(\Delta f)}{2 \Delta f^2} \right)$$

---

### 3. How to Determine the Parameters in Practice

To compute the numerical value of the phase noise, you need to find $S_{\text{th}}(\Delta f)$ and $K_{\text{push}}$ using simulation tools (such as Cadence Virtuoso):

1. **Find $S_{\text{th}}(\Delta f)$ (LDO Noise):**
   * Run a **Noise Analysis** (`.noise`) on the LDO regulator under the expected load current of the VCO.
   * Plot the output voltage noise PSD and find its value $S_{\text{th}}$ at the target offset frequency $\Delta f$.

2. **Find $K_{\text{push}}$ (VCO Supply Pushing):**
   * Run a **Periodic Steady-State (PSS)** simulation of the VCO.
   * Measure the oscillation frequency $f_{\text{osc1}}$ at nominal supply $V_{\text{out}}$.
   * Change the supply voltage slightly to $V_{\text{out}} + \Delta V$ (e.g., $\Delta V = 50\text{ mV}$) and measure the new frequency $f_{\text{osc2}}$.
   * Calculate the pushing factor:
     $$K_{\text{push}} \approx \frac{f_{\text{osc2}} - f_{\text{osc1}}}{\Delta V}$$

3. **Calculate Phase Noise:**
   * Plug $K_{\text{push}}$ and $S_{\text{th}}(\Delta f)$ into the formula above to find the phase noise contribution of the LDO at the offset frequency $\Delta f$. This value can then be root-sum-squared with the VCO's intrinsic phase noise to find the total phase noise.

---

### 4. Output Single-Sideband (SSB) Phase Noise
The standard Single-Sideband phase noise $\mathcal{L}(\Delta f)$ (in $\text{rad}^2/\text{Hz}$ or $\text{dBc/Hz}$) is given by:

$$\mathcal{L}(\Delta f) = \frac{1}{2} S_\phi(\Delta f) = \frac{1}{2} \left(\frac{K_{\text{push}}}{2\pi \Delta f}\right)^2 S_{\text{th}}$$

Alternatively, if using $K_{\text{push, Hz}} = \frac{\partial f_0}{\partial V_{\text{out}}}$ (in $\text{Hz/V}$):

$$\mathcal{L}(\Delta f) = \frac{K_{\text{push, Hz}}^2}{2 \, \Delta f^2} S_{\text{th}}$$

$$\mathcal{L}(\Delta f) = 10 \log_{10} \left[ \frac{K_{\text{push, Hz}}^2}{2 \, \Delta f^2} S_{\text{th}} \right]$$

---

### Summary Checklist to Compute It:
1. **Find/Measure $S_{\text{th}}$:** The output noise density of the LDO (in $\text{V}^2/\text{Hz}$).
2. **Find/Simulate $K_{\text{push}}$:** Sweep $V_{\text{out}}$ around its nominal operating point, measure $\Delta f_0$, and calculate $K_{\text{push, Hz}} = \frac{\Delta f_0}{\Delta V_{\text{out}}}$.
3. **Apply the formula:** Substitute into $\mathcal{L}(\Delta f) = \frac{K_{\text{push, Hz}}^2}{2 \, \Delta f^2} S_{\text{th}}$ at the offset frequency of interest $\Delta f$.

To compute the VCO output phase noise resulting from the thermal noise spectrum $S_{\text{th}}$ of the low-dropout (LDO) regulator, we analyze how supply noise is converted into phase fluctuations at nodes $X$ and $Y$. 

The conversion occurs through two primary mechanisms:
1. **Supply Pushing (Frequency Modulation)** — typically the dominant mechanism.
2. **Harmonic Folding & Asymmetry (Time-Variant Mixing)** via the Linear Time-Variant (LTV) / Hajimiri framework.

---

### 1. Dominant Mechanism: Supply Pushing (FM Theory)

#### A. Determine the Supply Pushing Factor ($K_{\text{push}}$)
The DC voltage drop across the inductors $L_1$ is negligible. Therefore, the average DC voltage at the oscillation nodes $X$ and $Y$ is set directly by the LDO output:
$$V_{X,\text{DC}} = V_{Y,\text{DC}} \approx V_{\text{out}}$$

The MOS varactors $M_{\text{v1}}$ and $M_{\text{v2}}$ have their gates tied to nodes $X$ and $Y$ and their source/drain/bulk terminals tied to $V_{\text{cont}}$. The average voltage across the varactors is:
$$V_{\text{var}} = V_{\text{out}} - V_{\text{cont}}$$

Because the oscillation frequency is:
$$\omega_0 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{L_1 C_{\text{tot}}}}$$
any variation in $V_{\text{out}}$ modulates $C_{\text{tot}}$ primarily via the varactor capacitance $C_{\text{var}}(V_{\text{var}})$. 

The **supply pushing factor** $K_{\text{push}}$ is defined as:
$$K_{\text{push}} = \frac{\partial \omega_0}{\partial V_{\text{out}}} = -\frac{\omega_0}{2 C_{\text{tot}}} \frac{\partial C_{\text{tot}}}{\partial V_{\text{out}}}$$

Since $V_{\text{var}} = V_{\text{out}} - V_{\text{cont}}$, we have:
$$\frac{\partial C_{\text{var}}}{\partial V_{\text{out}}} = -\frac{\partial C_{\text{var}}}{\partial V_{\text{cont}}}$$

If the varactors dominate the frequency sensitivity, the pushing factor is approximately equal to the VCO tuning sensitivity $K_{\text{VCO}}$:
$$|K_{\text{push}}| \approx K_{\text{VCO}} = \left|\frac{\partial \omega_0}{\partial V_{\text{cont}}}\right| \quad (\text{in rad/s/V})$$
*(Note: Additional minor contributions to $K_{\text{push}}$ arise from the voltage-dependent junction capacitances $C_{\text{db1,2}}$ of $M_1, M_2$ and amplitude-dependent capacitance via AM-to-PM conversion).*

---

#### B. Compute Phase Noise from $K_{\text{push}}$
Let the LDO generate a single-sided thermal voltage noise spectral density $S_{\text{th}}(\Delta f)$ (in $\text{V}^2/\text{Hz}$). 

1. **Frequency Fluctuations:**
   The noise voltage $v_n(t)$ at the LDO output creates instantaneous frequency fluctuations:
   $$\Delta\omega(t) = K_{\text{push}} v_n(t) \implies S_{\Delta\omega}(\Delta\omega) = K_{\text{push}}^2 S_{\text{th}}(\Delta\omega)$$

2. **Phase Fluctuations:**
   Because excess phase is the time integral of frequency ($\phi(t) = \int \Delta\omega(t) dt$), the transfer function from frequency deviation to phase is $1/s$:
   $$S_\phi(\Delta\omega) = \frac{S_{\Delta\omega}(\Delta\omega)}{\Delta\omega^2} = \frac{K_{\text{push}}^2}{\Delta\omega^2} S_{\text{th}}(\Delta\omega) \quad (\text{in rad}^2/\text{Hz})$$

3. **Single-Sideband Phase Noise $\mathcal{L}(\Delta\omega)$:**
   By standard convention, $\mathcal{L}(\Delta\omega) = \frac{1}{2} S_\phi(\Delta\omega)$:
   $$\mathcal{L}(\Delta\omega) = 10 \log_{10} \left( \frac{K_{\text{push}}^2}{2 \Delta\omega^2} S_{\text{th}}(\Delta\omega) \right) \quad (\text{in dBc/Hz})$$

   Equivalently, using cyclic frequency $\Delta f$ (with $K_{\text{push, Hz/V}} = \frac{K_{\text{push}}}{2\pi}$):
   $$\mathcal{L}(\Delta f) = 10 \log_{10} \left( \frac{K_{\text{push, Hz/V}}^2}{2 (\Delta f)^2} S_{\text{th}}(\Delta f) \right)$$

---

### 2. High-Frequency Noise Folding (LTV / Hajimiri Model)

Because the VCO is a periodic, time-varying (LTV) system, noise components from the LDO at harmonics of $\omega_0$ can fold into near-carrier phase noise:

$$\mathcal{L}(\Delta\omega) = \frac{1}{4 q_{\text{max}}^2 \Delta\omega^2} \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} c_n^2 S_{\text{th}}(n\omega_0)$$
where $q_{\text{max}} = C_{\text{tot}} V_{\text{tank}}$ is the maximum charge swing across the tank, and $c_n$ are the Fourier coefficients of the Impulse Sensitivity Function (ISF) $\Gamma(t)$ from the $V_{\text{out}}$ node.

* **$n = 0$ (DC/Low-Frequency Component):** 
  Matches the FM pushing derivation above, where $c_0 \propto K_{\text{push}}$.
* **$n = 2$ ($2\omega_0$ Folding):** 
  Because $V_{\text{out}}$ is a common-mode node, the cross-coupled pair switches twice per cycle, generating common-mode activity at $2\omega_0$. If the LDO exhibits high-frequency noise around $2\omega_0$, it folds down into the carrier via the coefficient $c_2$.
* **$n = 1$ ($\omega_0$ Asymmetry Component):** 
  In an ideally symmetric circuit, fundamental noise at $\omega_0$ is purely common-mode and rejected ($c_1 \approx 0$). However, any physical mismatch between inductors $L_1$, transistors $M_1/M_2$, or varactors converts common-mode supply noise at $\omega_0$ directly into differential phase noise:
  $$c_1 \propto \left( \frac{\Delta L}{L} + \frac{\Delta C}{C} + \frac{\Delta g_m}{g_m} \right)$$

---

### Step-by-Step Procedure for Practical Computation

1. **Obtain $S_{\text{th}}$:** Determine the LDO output noise voltage spectral density $S_{\text{th}}$ (in $\text{V}^2/\text{Hz}$) at the offset frequency $\Delta f$ (and optionally at $2f_0$).
2. **Find $K_{\text{push}}$:** 
   * **Analytically/Approximation:** Use $|K_{\text{push}}| \approx K_{\text{VCO}} = 2\pi \frac{\partial f_0}{\partial V_{\text{cont}}}$.
   * **Via Simulation:** Run a DC sweep or parametric transient simulation of $V_{\text{out}}$ by $\pm \Delta V$ and compute $K_{\text{push}} = 2\pi \frac{\Delta f_0}{\Delta V_{\text{out}}}$.
3. **Calculate Base Phase Noise:**
   $$\mathcal{L}(\Delta f) = \frac{K_{\text{push, Hz/V}}^2}{2 (\Delta f)^2} S_{\text{th}}(\Delta f)$$
4. **Include Folding/Mismatch (if high precision is required):** Use Periodic Steady-State (PSS) and Periodic Noise (PNoise) simulations in Cadence Spectre RF / ADS to capture the high-frequency folding terms ($c_1, c_2$).

To compute the VCO output phase noise resulting from the LDO thermal noise spectrum $S_{\text{th}}$, we analyze how voltage fluctuations on the supply rail ($V_{\text{out}}$) are converted into phase fluctuations at the oscillator output.

---

### 1. Primary Mechanism: Frequency Modulation via Supply Pushing

The predominant mechanism by which low-frequency supply noise produces phase noise is **supply pushing**—the modulation of the VCO oscillation frequency $\omega_{\text{osc}}$ by changes in the supply voltage $V_{\text{out}}$.

We define the supply pushing factor as:
$$K_{\text{push}} = \frac{\partial \omega_{\text{osc}}}{\partial V_{\text{out}}} \quad [\text{rad}/(\text{s}\cdot\text{V})] \quad \text{or} \quad K_{\text{push,Hz}} = \frac{\partial f_{\text{osc}}}{\partial V_{\text{out}}} = \frac{K_{\text{push}}}{2\pi} \quad [\text{Hz}/\text{V}]$$

---

### 2. Determining $K_{\text{push}}$ for this Topology

The oscillation frequency of the LC tank is:
$$\omega_{\text{osc}} \approx \frac{1}{\sqrt{L_1 C_{\text{tot}}}}$$
where $C_{\text{tot}}$ is the total capacitance seen at each tank node ($X$ and $Y$). $C_{\text{tot}}$ depends on $V_{\text{out}}$ through several components:

#### A. Varactor Tuning Sensitivity (Dominant Contributor)
* The inductors $L_1$ carry the DC bias current to the cross-coupled pair $M_1, M_2$. Because ideal inductors have zero DC resistance (and real inductors have negligible resistance), the DC voltage at nodes $X$ and $Y$ is:
  $$V_{X,\text{DC}} = V_{Y,\text{DC}} = V_{\text{out}}$$
* The varactors $M_{\text{v1}}$ and $M_{\text{v2}}$ have their gates connected to nodes $X$ and $Y$, and their source/drain terminals tied to the control voltage $V_{\text{cont}}$.
* Thus, the DC voltage across each varactor is:
  $$V_{\text{var}} = V_{\text{out}} - V_{\text{cont}}$$
* Differentiating with respect to $V_{\text{out}}$ and $V_{\text{cont}}$:
  $$\frac{\partial V_{\text{var}}}{\partial V_{\text{out}}} = 1 = -\frac{\partial V_{\text{var}}}{\partial V_{\text{cont}}}$$
* Therefore, the pushing factor due to the varactors is directly equal in magnitude to the VCO tuning gain $K_{\text{VCO}}$:
  $$K_{\text{push,var}} = \frac{\partial \omega_{\text{osc}}}{\partial V_{\text{out}}}\Bigg|_{\text{var}} = -\frac{\partial \omega_{\text{osc}}}{\partial V_{\text{cont}}} = -K_{\text{VCO}}$$
  This makes the varactors typically the **largest contributor** to supply pushing in this circuit.

#### B. Nonlinear Parasitic Capacitances
* **Drain-bulk junction capacitances ($C_{db1}, C_{db2}$):** Since the drains are at $V_{\text{out}}$ and the substrate is at ground, the reverse bias is $V_{\text{out}}$. As $V_{\text{out}}$ increases, the depletion region widens and $C_{db}$ decreases, slightly increasing $\omega_{\text{osc}}$:
  $$\frac{\partial C_{db}}{\partial V_{\text{out}}} < 0 \implies \frac{\partial \omega_{\text{osc}}}{\partial C_{db}}\frac{\partial C_{db}}{\partial V_{\text{out}}} > 0$$
* **Switched-capacitor banks ($B_1, B_2$):** For switches that are turned OFF, the reverse-biased junction capacitance of the switch transistors also depends on $V_{\text{out}}$.

#### C. Finite Tail Impedance
* If the tail current source $I_{\text{VCO}}$ has a finite output resistance $r_O$, variations in $V_{\text{out}}$ modulate the tail current:
  $$\Delta I_{\text{VCO}} \approx \frac{\Delta V_{\text{out}}}{r_O}$$
  This current variation causes additional frequency shifting through current pushing ($\partial \omega_{\text{osc}}/\partial I_{\text{VCO}}$).

Summing all contributions gives the net pushing factor:
$$K_{\text{push}} = -\frac{\omega_{\text{osc}}}{2 C_{\text{tot}}} \frac{\partial C_{\text{tot}}}{\partial V_{\text{out}}} + \frac{\partial \omega_{\text{osc}}}{\partial I_{\text{VCO}}}\frac{1}{r_O} \approx -K_{\text{VCO}}$$

---

### 3. Calculating the Phase Noise $\mathcal{L}(\Delta f)$

Let $S_{\text{th}}$ denote the single-sided power spectral density (PSD) of the LDO output voltage noise in $\text{V}^2/\text{Hz}$.

1. **Frequency Fluctuation Spectrum:**
   The voltage noise modulates the instantaneous frequency:
   $$\Delta\omega(t) = K_{\text{push}} \cdot v_{\text{out,noise}}(t)$$
   The spectral density of frequency fluctuations is:
   $$S_{\Delta\omega}(\Delta f) = K_{\text{push}}^2 S_{\text{th}}(\Delta f) \quad [(\text{rad}/\text{s})^2/\text{Hz}]$$

2. **Phase Fluctuation Spectrum:**
   Since phase is the time integral of frequency ($\phi(t) = \int \Delta\omega(t) dt$), integration in the frequency domain corresponds to dividing by $\Delta\omega^2 = (2\pi \Delta f)^2$:
   $$S_{\phi}(\Delta f) = \frac{S_{\Delta\omega}(\Delta f)}{(2\pi \Delta f)^2} = \frac{K_{\text{push}}^2}{(2\pi \Delta f)^2} S_{\text{th}}(\Delta f) = \frac{K_{\text{push,Hz}}^2}{\Delta f^2} S_{\text{th}}(\Delta f) \quad [\text{rad}^2/\text{Hz}]$$

3. **Single-Sideband (SSB) Phase Noise:**
   Under the narrow-band frequency modulation approximation, the single-sideband phase noise $\mathcal{L}(\Delta f)$ (in $\text{dBc}/\text{Hz}$) at an offset frequency $\Delta f$ from the carrier is:
   $$\mathcal{L}(\Delta f) = 10 \log_{10} \left[ \frac{1}{2} S_{\phi}(\Delta f) \right]$$

   $$\mathcal{L}(\Delta f) = 10 \log_{10} \left[ \frac{K_{\text{push}}^2}{2 (2\pi \Delta f)^2} S_{\text{th}}(\Delta f) \right] = 10 \log_{10} \left[ \frac{K_{\text{push,Hz}}^2}{2 \Delta f^2} S_{\text{th}}(\Delta f) \right]$$

   If the varactor dominates ($K_{\text{push}} \approx -K_{\text{VCO}}$), this simplifies to:
   $$\mathcal{L}(\Delta f) \approx 10 \log_{10} \left[ \frac{K_{\text{VCO}}^2}{2 (2\pi \Delta f)^2} S_{\text{th}}(\Delta f) \right]$$

Because thermal noise $S_{\text{th}}$ is white (flat across frequency), the resulting phase noise exhibits a characteristic **$1/f^2$** slope ($-\text{20 dB/dec}$) versus offset frequency $\Delta f$.

---

### 4. Secondary Conversion Mechanisms (High-Frequency Noise)

While the low-frequency FM path above is the dominant contributor, white thermal noise from the LDO also contains high-frequency components:

1. **Noise near $2\omega_{\text{osc}}$ (Harmonic Mixing):**
   * The common-mode node of the cross-coupled pair naturally oscillates at $2\omega_{\text{osc}}$.
   * Thermal noise from $V_{\text{out}}$ near $2\omega_{\text{osc}}$ mixes with this second harmonic and downconverts into phase noise around the fundamental carrier $\omega_{\text{osc}}$.
2. **Noise near $\omega_{\text{osc}}$ (Circuit Asymmetry):**
   * Ideally, noise from $V_{\text{out}}$ is purely common-mode and is rejected by the differential tank.
   * Any physical mismatch between the two halves ($\Delta L_1$, varactor mismatch, or $M_1/M_2$ mismatch) converts common-mode noise at $\omega_{\text{osc}}$ directly into differential phase noise.

---

### Summary of Computation Steps
1. **Find/Measure $S_{\text{th}}$:** Obtain the output noise spectral density of the LDO ($\text{V}^2/\text{Hz}$) at the offset frequency of interest.
2. **Determine $K_{\text{push}}$:** Calculate or simulate $\frac{\partial f_{\text{osc}}}{\partial V_{\text{out}}}$ across the tuning range (approximated by $K_{\text{VCO}}$ if varactors dominate).
3. **Evaluate Phase Noise:** Compute $\mathcal{L}(\Delta f) = 10 \log_{10} \left( \frac{K_{\text{push,Hz}}^2}{2 \Delta f^2} S_{\text{th}} \right)$.

Thus, the phase noise power spectral density $S_\phi(\Delta f)$ (in $\text{rad}^2/\text{Hz}$) at an offset frequency $\Delta f$ is:

The single-sideband (SSB) phase noise $\mathcal{L}(\Delta f)$ (in $\text{dBc/Hz}$) is given by:

$$\mathcal{L}(\Delta f) = 10 \log_{10} \left( \frac{1}{2} S_\phi(\Delta f) \right) = 10 \log_{10} \left[ \frac{K_{\text{push,Hz}}^2}{2\Delta f^2} S_{\text{th}}(\Delta f) \right]$$

### 2. Physical Origin and Calculation of $K_{\text{push}}$

To compute the phase noise quantitatively, we must find $K_{\text{push}}$ from the circuit parameters:

#### A. DC Common-Mode Level at Nodes $X$ and $Y$
Because inductors $L_1$ carry the DC current $I_{\text{VCO}}/2$ and have negligible DC series resistance:
$$V_{X,\text{DC}} = V_{Y,\text{DC}} \approx V_{\text{out}}$$
Any low-frequency variation $\Delta V_{\text{out}}$ shifts the common-mode voltage of nodes $X$ and $Y$ directly:
$$\Delta V_{X,Y,\text{CM}} = \Delta V_{\text{out}}$$

#### B. Varactor Sensitivity (Dominant Mechanism)
The varactors $M_{v1}$ and $M_{v2}$ have their control terminal connected to $V_{\text{cont}}$ and their other terminals connected to nodes $X$ and $Y$. The effective tuning voltage across the varactors is:
$$V_{\text{var}} = V_{\text{cont}} - V_{\text{out}}$$
Since the resonance frequency is $\omega_{\text{osc}} \approx 1/\sqrt{L_1 C_{\text{tot}}}$, a change in $V_{\text{out}}$ alters the varactor capacitance in the opposite direction of $V_{\text{cont}}$:
$$\frac{\partial C_{\text{var}}}{\partial V_{\text{out}}} = -\frac{\partial C_{\text{var}}}{\partial V_{\text{cont}}}$$
Consequently, the varactor contribution to pushing is directly tied to the VCO tuning gain $K_{\text{VCO}}$:
$$K_{\text{push,var}} \approx -K_{\text{VCO}} = -\frac{\partial \omega_{\text{osc}}}{\partial V_{\text{cont}}}$$
*In designs with high tuning sensitivity ($K_{\text{VCO}}$), varactor modulation is typically the dominant contributor to supply pushing.*

#### C. Parasitic Capacitance Modulation
- **Drain-Bulk Junction Capacitance ($C_{db}$):** The drains of $M_1$ and $M_2$ sit at $V_{\text{out}}$. As $V_{\text{out}}$ increases, the reverse bias across the drain-bulk junctions increases, decreasing $C_{db}$ and slightly increasing $\omega_{\text{osc}}$:
  $$\frac{\partial C_{db}}{\partial V_{\text{out}}} < 0 \implies K_{\text{push}, Cdb} > 0$$
- **Switched-Capacitor Banks ($B_1, B_2$):** Depending on whether the switches are ON or OFF, the junction and overlap capacitances of the MOS switches also exhibit slight voltage dependency on $V_{\text{out}}$.

#### D. Tail Current Modulation (AM-to-PM Conversion)
If the tail current source $I_{\text{VCO}}$ has a finite output impedance $r_O$:
$$\Delta I_{\text{VCO}} \approx \frac{\Delta V_{\text{out}}}{r_O}$$
This modulates the oscillation amplitude $V_{\text{tank}} \approx \frac{4}{\pi} I_{\text{VCO}} R_{\text{tank}}$. Because the varactors and junction capacitors are nonlinear, a change in amplitude shifts their cycle-averaged capacitance, contributing further to $K_{\text{push}}$.

$$K_{\text{push}} = \left. \frac{\partial \omega_{\text{osc}}}{\partial V_{\text{out}}} \right|_{\text{net}} \approx -K_{\text{VCO}} + \frac{\partial \omega_{\text{osc}}}{\partial C_{db}}\frac{\partial C_{db}}{\partial V_{\text{out}}} + \left(\frac{\partial \omega_{\text{osc}}}{\partial V_{\text{tank}}}\frac{\partial V_{\text{tank}}}{\partial I_{\text{VCO}}}\frac{\partial I_{\text{VCO}}}{\partial V_{\text{out}}}\right)$$

- $\Gamma_2$ is the second-harmonic Fourier coefficient of the oscillator's Impulse Sensitivity Function (ISF).
- $q_{\text{max}} = C_{\text{tot}} V_{\text{tank}}$ is the maximum charge swing across the tank.

*Note:* In practice, the LDO output impedance drops or is heavily bypassed by a decoupling capacitor at $2\omega_0$, making the low-frequency pushing mechanism ($K_{\text{push}}$) the dominant contributor to close-in phase noise.

1. **Obtain $S_{\text{th}}(\Delta f)$:** Measure or simulate the output noise spectral density of the LDO at offset $\Delta f$.
2. **Determine $K_{\text{push}}$:** 
   - *Analytically:* Approximate $K_{\text{push}} \approx -K_{\text{VCO}}$ (if varactors dominate).
   - *In Simulation:* Run a Periodic Steady-State (PSS) analysis while varying $V_{\text{out}}$ by a small $\Delta V$ to find $K_{\text{push,Hz}} = \Delta f_{\text{osc}} / \Delta V_{\text{out}}$.
3. **Calculate Output Phase Noise:**
   $$\mathcal{L}(\Delta f) = 10 \log_{10} \left[ \frac{K_{\text{push,Hz}}^2}{2\Delta f^2} S_{\text{th}}(\Delta f) \right] \quad [\text{dBc/Hz}]$$

To compute the VCO output phase noise resulting from the LDO's thermal noise, you need to follow a process based on the concept of **supply pushing**.

The LDO's thermal noise ($S_{th}$) manifests as voltage fluctuations on the supply line ($V_{out}$). Because the oscillation frequency of a practical VCO depends on its supply voltage, these voltage fluctuations cause frequency fluctuations, which ultimately result in phase noise.

Here is the step-by-step procedure:

### 1. Determine the Supply Pushing Factor ($K_{push}$)
The first step is to characterize how sensitive the VCO's frequency is to changes in the supply voltage. This is known as the supply pushing factor, $K_{push}$.
*   **Definition:** $K_{push} = \frac{\partial f_{osc}}{\partial V_{out}}$ (measured in Hz/V).
*   **How to find it:** This is typically done via circuit simulation (e.g., SPICE). You sweep the LDO output voltage $V_{out}$ by a small amount (e.g., $\pm 10\text{--}50\text{ mV}$) around its nominal value and measure the resulting change in the oscillation frequency $f_{osc}$. The slope of this curve is $K_{push}$.

### 2. Calculate the Frequency Noise Spectrum
The LDO's voltage noise spectral density $S_{LDO}(f)$ (which you've called $S_{th}$, in $V^2/Hz$) is converted into frequency noise spectral density $S_{\Delta f}(f)$ through the pushing factor. Since power spectral density scales with the square of the gain:
$$S_{\Delta f}(f_m) = K_{push}^2 \cdot S_{LDO}(f_m)$$
*   Where $f_m$ is the offset frequency from the carrier.
*   Units: $\text{Hz}^2/\text{Hz}$.

### 3. Convert Frequency Noise to Phase Noise
Phase is the integral of frequency. In the frequency domain, integration corresponds to a $1/f$ operation for amplitude, or a $1/f^2$ operation for power spectral density. The phase noise spectrum $S_{\phi}(f_m)$ is related to the frequency noise spectrum by:
$$S_{\phi}(f_m) = \frac{S_{\Delta f}(f_m)}{f_m^2} = \frac{K_{push}^2 \cdot S_{LDO}(f_m)}{f_m^2}$$
*   Units: $\text{rad}^2/\text{Hz}$.

### 4. Express in Standard Phase Noise Units ($\mathcal{L}$)
Phase noise is most commonly expressed in $\text{dBc/Hz}$ (decibels relative to the carrier per Hertz). By convention, $\mathcal{L}(f_m)$ represents the noise in one sideband, which is half of the total phase fluctuations:

Here is the step-by-step procedure:

### 1. Determine the Supply Pushing Figure ($K_{push}$)
The first step is to quantify how sensitive the VCO's oscillation frequency ($f_{osc}$) is to changes in the supply voltage ($V_{out}$). This sensitivity is called the supply pushing figure, denoted as $K_{push}$:

$$K_{push} = \frac{\partial f_{osc}}{\partial V_{out}} \quad \text{[units: Hz/V]}$$

In the circuit shown, $V_{out}$ affects the frequency because:
*   The parasitic capacitances of the cross-coupled pair ($M_1, M_2$) are voltage-dependent.
*   The average voltage across the varactors ($M_{v1}, M_{v2}$) changes with $V_{out}$, altering their effective capacitance.
*   If the tail current source $I_{VCO}$ has finite output impedance, changes in $V_{out}$ change the tail current, which in turn changes the transconductance and parasitic capacitances of the switching pair.

You can find $K_{push}$ via simulation by performing a DC sweep of $V_{out}$ and measuring the resulting change in the steady-state oscillation frequency.

### 2. Relate Supply Noise to Frequency Fluctuations
The LDO generates thermal noise with a power spectral density (PSD) of $S_{th}(f)$ (units: $V^2/Hz$). This voltage noise causes a corresponding noise in the instantaneous frequency of the VCO.

The PSD of the frequency fluctuations, $S_{\Delta f}(f)$, is calculated by multiplying the voltage noise PSD by the square of the pushing figure:

$$S_{\Delta f}(f) = K_{push}^2 \cdot S_{th}(f) \quad \text{[units: } Hz^2/Hz]$$

### 3. Compute the Phase Noise
Phase noise, $\mathcal{L}(\Delta f)$, is defined as the ratio of the noise power in a 1-Hz bandwidth at an offset frequency $\Delta f$ from the carrier to the total carrier power. 

There is a fundamental mathematical relationship between frequency fluctuations and phase noise: phase is the integral of frequency, which in the frequency domain corresponds to a $1/f^2$ relationship.

The phase noise at an offset frequency $\Delta f$ is given by:

$$\mathcal{L}(\Delta f) = \frac{S_{\Delta f}(\Delta f)}{2 (\Delta f)^2}$$

Substituting the expression from Step 2:

$$\mathcal{L}(\Delta f) = \frac{K_{push}^2 \cdot S_{th}(\Delta f)}{2 (\Delta f)^2}$$

2.  **Identify $S_{th}$** of the LDO at the specific offset frequency $\Delta f$ (in $V^2/Hz$).

Since frequency is the time derivative of phase, small-signal frequency modulation by the LDO noise $v_{n,\text{LDO}}(t)$ integrates to produce excess phase $\phi(t)$:
$$\Delta \omega_{\text{osc}}(t) = K_{\text{VCO}} \, v_{n,\text{LDO}}(t) \implies \phi(t) = K_{\text{VCO}} \int v_{n,\text{LDO}}(t)\,dt$$

In the frequency domain (at an offset frequency $\Delta \omega$ from the carrier $\omega_0$), the transfer function from $V_{\text{out}}$ to output phase $\Phi$ is:
$$\frac{\Phi}{V_{\text{out}}}(s) = \frac{K_{\text{VCO}}}{s} \implies \left| \frac{\Phi}{V_{\text{out}}}(j\Delta \omega) \right|^2 = \frac{K_{\text{VCO}}^2}{\Delta \omega^2}$$

#### **A. Phase Power Spectral Density, $S_\phi(\Delta \omega)$**
Multiplying the input noise PSD $S_{\text{th}}$ by the squared magnitude of the transfer function gives the total phase noise PSD:
$$S_\phi(\Delta \omega) = \frac{K_{\text{VCO}}^2}{\Delta \omega^2} S_{\text{th}}$$

$$\mathcal{L}(\Delta f)\big|_{\text{dBc/Hz}} = 10 \log_{10}\!\left( \frac{K_{\text{VCO}}^2 S_{\text{th}}}{4 \Delta \omega^2} \right) \quad \text{or} \quad 10 \log_{10}\!\left( \frac{K_{\text{VCO}}^2 S_{\text{th}}}{2 \Delta \omega^2} \right)$$

   $$V_{\text{var}} = V_{\text{out}} - V_{\text{cont}}$$

   Because the varactor capacitance depends only on the voltage *difference* $(V_{\text{out}} - V_{\text{cont}})$, a small change in $V_{\text{out}}$ alters the oscillation frequency by the exact same magnitude (with opposite polarity) as a small change in $V_{\text{cont}}$. $$v_n(t) = \sqrt{2 S_{\text{th}}(\Delta f)} \cos(\Delta \omega \, t)$$

This modulates the VCO’s instantaneous oscillation frequency around its carrier $\omega_0$:
$$\omega_{\text{osc}}(t) = \omega_0 + K_{\text{sup}} \sqrt{2 S_{\text{th}}(\Delta f)} \cos(\Delta \omega \, t)$$

Integrating frequency deviation yields the excess phase $\phi(t)$:
$$\phi(t) = \int \big[\omega_{\text{osc}}(t) - \omega_0\big]\,dt = \frac{K_{\text{sup}} \sqrt{2 S_{\text{th}}(\Delta f)}}{\Delta \omega} \sin(\Delta \omega \, t)$$

Since $|\phi(t)| \ll 1\text{ rad}$ (narrowband FM), the differential VCO output $v_{\text{VCO}}(t) = V_0 \cos[\omega_0 t + \phi(t)]$ can be expanded as:
$$\begin{aligned}
v_{\text{VCO}}(t) &\approx V_0 \cos(\omega_0 t) - V_0 \phi(t) \sin(\omega_0 t) \\
&= V_0 \cos(\omega_0 t) + \frac{V_0 K_{\text{sup}} \sqrt{2 S_{\text{th}}(\Delta f)}}{2 \Delta \omega} \Big[\cos(\omega_0 + \Delta \omega)t - \cos(\omega_0 - \Delta \omega)t\Big]
\end{aligned}$$

The **single-sideband (SSB) phase noise** $\mathcal{L}(\Delta \omega)$ is the ratio of the power in one sideband (per $\text{Hz}$) to the carrier power ($V_0^2 / 2$):
$$\mathcal{L}(\Delta \omega) = \frac{\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{V_0 K_{\text{sup}} \sqrt{2 S_{\text{th}}(\Delta f)}}{2 \Delta \omega}\right)^2}{\frac{1}{2} V_0^2} = \frac{K_{\text{sup}}^2 \, S_{\text{th}}(\Delta f)}{2 (\Delta \omega)^2}$$

Substituting $|K_{\text{sup}}| \approx K_{\text{VCO}}$:
$$\mathcal{L}(\Delta \omega) \approx \frac{K_{\text{VCO}}^2 \, S_{\text{th}}(\Delta f)}{2 (\Delta \omega)^2}$$

If the VCO gain is expressed in $\text{Hz/V}$ as $K_{f,\text{VCO}} = \frac{\partial f_{\text{osc}}}{\partial V_{\text{cont}}} = \frac{K_{\text{VCO}}}{2\pi}$, the $2\pi$ factors cancel:
$$\mathcal{L}(\Delta f) \approx \frac{K_{f,\text{VCO}}^2 \, S_{\text{th}}(\Delta f)}{2 (\Delta f)^2} \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \mathcal{L}(\Delta f)\big|_{\text{dBc/Hz}} = 10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{K_{f,\text{VCO}}^2 \, S_{\text{th}}(\Delta f)}{2 (\Delta f)^2}\right)$$

---

#### Method B: Phase-Domain Transfer Function (Equivalent)
Treating the VCO as an ideal voltage-to-phase integrator with transfer function $\Phi_{\text{out}}(s)/V_{\text{out}}(s) = K_{\text{sup}}/s$, the one-sided PSD of the excess phase is:
$$S_\phi(\Delta \omega) = \left|\frac{K_{\text{sup}}}{j\Delta \omega}\right|^2 S_{\text{th}}(\Delta \omega) = \frac{K_{\text{sup}}^2}{(\Delta \omega)^2} S_{\text{th}}(\Delta \omega)$$

Using the standard IEEE small-angle relation $\mathcal{L}(\Delta \omega) = \frac{1}{2} S_\phi(\Delta \omega)$ gives the identical result:
$$\mathcal{L}(\Delta \omega) = \frac{K_{\text{sup}}^2 \, S_{\text{th}}(\Delta \omega)}{2 (\Delta \omega)^2} \approx \frac{K_{\text{VCO}}^2 \, S_{\text{th}}(\Delta \omega)}{2 (\Delta \omega)^2}$$

*(Note: If $S_{\text{th}}$ is defined as a **two-sided** spectral density $\tilde{S}_{\text{th}} = S_{\text{th}}/2$, then $\mathcal{L}(\Delta \omega) = \frac{K_{\text{VCO}}^2 \tilde{S}_{\text{th}}(\Delta \omega)}{(\Delta \omega)^2}$.)*

---

### High-Frequency Noise & Simulation Remarks
* **Noise near $f_0$:** Enters $V_{\text{out}}$ as a common-mode disturbance; by circuit symmetry, it is rejected at the differential output $V_X - V_Y$ to first order.
* **Noise near $2f_0$:** Common-mode noise at $2f_0 \pm \Delta f$ can in principle mix down to $f_0 \pm \Delta f$ (via varactor parametric modulation or parasitic capacitance at the tail node). In an RF simulator (e.g., SpectreRF **PSS + PNoise**), injecting $S_{\text{th}}$ at $V_{\text{out}}$ automatically sums both the baseband ($k=0$) FM contribution and any harmonic ($k=2, 4, \dots$) folding terms.

To compute the VCO output phase noise caused by the LDO’s output thermal noise $S_{\text{th}}$ (assumed to be the one-sided voltage noise power spectral density in $\text{V}^2/\text{Hz}$), we break the analysis into two steps: **(1) finding the VCO frequency sensitivity to $V_{\text{out}}$**, and **(2) converting that frequency modulation into output phase noise**.

---

### 1. Frequency Sensitivity of the VCO to $V_{\text{out}}$

1. **DC / Low-Frequency Bias of Nodes $X$ and $Y$:**  
   At low offset frequencies $\Delta f$ ($\Delta\omega = 2\pi\Delta f \ll \omega_0$), the impedance of the tank inductors $L_1$ is negligible ($|j\Delta\omega L_1| \approx 0$). Consequently, the average (DC) voltage at nodes $X$ and $Y$ equals $V_{\text{out}}$, and any slow noise fluctuation on $V_{\text{out}}$ appears directly at $X$ and $Y$.

2. **Modulation of the MOS Varactors ($M_{\text{v1}}, M_{\text{v2}}$):**  
   * The gates of varactors $M_{\text{v1}}$ and $M_{\text{v2}}$ are connected to nodes $X$ and $Y$ (average voltage $V_{\text{out}}$), while their source/drain terminals are tied to $V_{\text{cont}}$ (which is referenced to ground).
   * Meanwhile, the tail current source $I_{\text{VCO}}$ fixes the oscillation amplitude $V_A$ (in the current-limited regime) and forces the common-source node of $M_1, M_2$ to track slow variations in $V_{\text{out}}$ so that the average $V_{GS}$ of $M_1, M_2$ stays constant. Furthermore, the coarse-tuning banks $B_1$ and $B_2$ use linear capacitors switched to ground, which reduce $K_{\text{VCO}}$ overall without introducing voltage-dependent capacitance of their own to first order.
   * Thus, the instantaneous voltages across the varactors are:
     $$V_{M_{\text{v1}}}(t) = V_X(t) - V_{\text{cont}} = (V_{\text{out}} - V_{\text{cont}}) + V_A \cos(\omega_0 t)$$
     $$V_{M_{\text{v2}}}(t) = V_Y(t) - V_{\text{cont}} = (V_{\text{out}} - V_{\text{cont}}) - V_A \cos(\omega_0 t)$$

3. **Sensitivity Equals $-K_{\text{VCO}}$:**  
   Because the effective varactor capacitance depends strictly on the difference $(V_{\text{out}} - V_{\text{cont}})$, a low-frequency variation at $V_{\text{out}}$ modulates the oscillation frequency in the **exact same manner** (with opposite sign) as a variation at $V_{\text{cont}}$:
   $$\frac{\partial \omega_{\text{osc}}}{\partial V_{\text{out}}} = -\frac{\partial \omega_{\text{osc}}}{\partial V_{\text{cont}}} = -K_{\text{VCO}}$$
   *(Note: If secondary effects—such as the drain-to-bulk junction capacitances of $M_1, M_2$ or channel-length modulation—are significant, $K_{\text{VCO}}$ can be replaced by the total supply-pushing gain $K_{\text{supply}} = \left|\partial\omega_{\text{osc}}/\partial V_{\text{out}}\right|$; in this topology, $K_{\text{VCO}}$ is the dominant mechanism.)*

---

### 2. Computing the VCO Output Phase Noise

Only low-frequency thermal noise on $V_{\text{out}}$ at offset frequency $\Delta\omega = 2\pi\Delta f$ dominates the phase noise at $\omega_0 \pm \Delta\omega$. We can derive the resulting phase noise using either the **phase-domain transfer function** or **narrowband FM modulation**:

#### Method A: Linear Phase-Domain Transfer Function
Since instantaneous excess angular frequency is the time derivative of excess phase $\phi_{\text{out}}(t)$, small-signal noise $v_{n,\text{out}}(t)$ at $V_{\text{out}}$ produces:
$$\frac{d\phi_{\text{out}}(t)}{dt} = -K_{\text{VCO}}\,v_{n,\text{out}}(t) \implies \frac{\Phi_{\text{out}}(s)}{V_{n,\text{out}}(s)} = -\frac{K_{\text{VCO}}}{s}$$

For a one-sided thermal noise spectrum $S_{\text{th}}$ (in $\text{V}^2/\text{Hz}$, evaluated at offset $\Delta\omega$), the **one-sided phase noise spectrum** $S_{\phi}(\Delta\omega)$ (in $\text{rad}^2/\text{Hz}$) is:
$$S_{\phi}(\Delta\omega) = \left|\frac{-K_{\text{VCO}}}{j\Delta\omega}\right|^2 S_{\text{th}} = \frac{K_{\text{VCO}}^2\,S_{\text{th}}}{\Delta\omega^2}$$

By the standard definition of **single-sideband (SSB) phase noise** relative to the carrier power, $\mathcal{L}(\Delta\omega) = \frac{1}{2} S_{\phi}(\Delta\omega)$:
$$\mathcal{L}(\Delta\omega) = \frac{K_{\text{VCO}}^2\,S_{\text{th}}}{2\,\Delta\omega^2}$$

#### Method B: Narrowband FM (Equivalent Sinusoid) Derivation
Alternatively, represent the thermal noise in a $1\text{-Hz}$ bandwidth centered at offset $\omega_m = \Delta\omega$ as an equivalent sinusoid $v_n(t) = V_m \cos(\omega_m t)$. Equating its average power to $S_{\text{th}} \cdot (1\text{ Hz})$ gives:
$$\frac{V_m^2}{2} = S_{\text{th}} \implies V_m = \sqrt{2 S_{\text{th}}}$$

Assuming narrowband FM ($\frac{K_{\text{VCO}} V_m}{\omega_m} \ll 1$), the differential VCO output voltage is:
$$\begin{aligned}
V_{\text{VCO}}(t) &= V_0 \cos\!\left[\omega_0 t - \frac{K_{\text{VCO}} V_m}{\omega_m} \sin(\omega_m t)\right] \\
&\approx V_0 \cos(\omega_0 t) + \frac{K_{\text{VCO}} V_m}{2\omega_m} V_0 \cos(\omega_0 - \omega_m)t - \frac{K_{\text{VCO}} V_m}{2\omega_m} V_0 \cos(\omega_0 + \omega_m)t
\end{aligned}$$

Dividing the power of a single sideband at $\omega_0 + \omega_m$ by the carrier power at $\omega_0$ gives the same result:
$$\mathcal{L}(\omega_m) = \frac{\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{K_{\text{VCO}} V_m}{2\omega_m} V_0\right)^2}{\frac{1}{2} V_0^2} = \frac{K_{\text{VCO}}^2 V_m^2}{4\,\omega_m^2} = \frac{K_{\text{VCO}}^2 (2 S_{\text{th}})}{4\,\omega_m^2} = \frac{K_{\text{VCO}}^2\,S_{\text{th}}}{2\,\omega_m^2}$$

---

### Summary & Unit Conventions

Expressed in $\text{dBc/Hz}$ at offset $\Delta f$ ($\Delta\omega = 2\pi\Delta f$):
$$\mathcal{L}(\Delta f)\Big|_{\text{dBc/Hz}} = 10 \log_{10}\!\left(\frac{K_{\text{VCO}}^2\,S_{\text{th}}}{2\,\Delta\omega^2}\right)$$

* **If $K_{\text{VCO}}$ is in $\text{rad}\cdot\text{s}^{-1}\cdot\text{V}^{-1}$** and $\Delta\omega = 2\pi\Delta f$ is in $\text{rad/s}$:
  $$\mathcal{L}(\Delta\omega) = \frac{K_{\text{VCO}}^2\,S_{\text{th}}}{2\,\Delta\omega^2}$$
* **If $\hat{K}_{\text{VCO}} = \frac{K_{\text{VCO}}}{2\pi}$ is in $\text{Hz/V}$** and $\Delta f$ is in $\text{Hz}$ (the $2\pi$ factors cancel):
  $$\mathcal{L}(\Delta f) = \frac{\hat{K}_{\text{VCO}}^2\,S_{\text{th}}}{2\,\Delta f^2}$$

*(Additional circuit notes: High-frequency LDO noise near $\omega_0$ enters nodes $X$ and $Y$ as a **common-mode** signal and is rejected by the differential output, while noise near $2\omega_0$ is typically heavily attenuated by the LDO output/decoupling capacitance and lacks the large $1/\Delta\omega^2$ FM integration gain that makes baseband noise at $\Delta\omega$ dominant.)*

---

### 1. Determine the VCO’s Supply Sensitivity ($K_{\text{sup}} = \partial \omega_{\text{osc}} / \partial V_{\text{out}}$)

Consider a low-frequency noise component on $V_{\text{out}}$ at an offset frequency $\Delta \omega = 2\pi \Delta f$ (where $\Delta \omega \ll \omega_0$):

1. **Direct Modulation of the Varactors ($M_{\text{v1}}, M_{\text{v2}}$) — Dominant Mechanism:**
   * Because the tank inductors $L_1$ have zero DC voltage drop and negligible impedance at low offset frequencies ($\Delta \omega L_1 \approx 0$), the average voltage at nodes $X$ and $Y$ tracks $V_{\text{out}}$ directly:
     $$\overline{V_X} = \overline{V_Y} = V_{\text{out}}$$
   * The gates of MOS varactors $M_{\text{v1}}$ and $M_{\text{v2}}$ are connected to $X$ and $Y$, while their source/drain terminals are connected to $V_{\text{cont}}$. Thus, the average bias voltage across both varactors is:
     $$V_{\text{var}} = V_{\text{out}} - V_{\text{cont}}$$
   * Meanwhile, the coarse switched-capacitor banks $B_1$ and $B_2$ use linear (voltage-independent) metal capacitors (which also block DC from the switches when open). Their purpose is to cover coarse tuning so that $M_{\text{v1}}$ and $M_{\text{v2}}$—and hence the VCO gain $K_{\text{VCO}}$—can be kept small; they do not contribute DC voltage sensitivity.
   * Since $V_{\text{out}}$ and $V_{\text{cont}}$ appear symmetrically with opposite signs across both varactors, a slow perturbation on $V_{\text{out}}$ modulates the varactor capacitance with the **exact same magnitude** as a perturbation on $V_{\text{cont}}$:
     $$\left| \frac{\partial \omega_{\text{osc}}}{\partial V_{\text{out}}} \right|_{\text{var}} = \left| \frac{\partial \omega_{\text{osc}}}{\partial V_{\text{cont}}} \right| = K_{\text{VCO}}$$

2. **Secondary Mechanisms (Exact Supply Pushing $K_{\text{sup}}$):**
   * Variations in $V_{\text{out}}$ also change the reverse bias across the drain-to-bulk junction capacitances ($C_{db}$) of $M_1$ and $M_2$. Additionally, because the common-source tail node tracks $V_{\text{out}} - V_{GS}$, the finite output resistance of $I_{\text{VCO}}$ allows $V_{\text{out}}$ to slightly modulate the tail current and oscillation amplitude, shifting the effective tank capacitance (AM-to-PM conversion).
   * In general, all low-frequency mechanisms combine into a total **supply sensitivity** (supply pushing factor):
     $$K_{\text{sup}} = \frac{\partial \omega_{\text{osc}}}{\partial V_{\text{out}}} \qquad (\text{in rad}\cdot\text{s}^{-1}\cdot\text{V}^{-1})$$
     where $|K_{\text{sup}}| \approx K_{\text{VCO}}$ when the varactors dominate the tank's voltage-dependent capacitance (or $K_{\text{sup}}$ can be extracted directly in simulation by sweeping $V_{\text{out}}$ slightly around its nominal DC value).

---

### 2. Compute the Output Phase Noise from $S_{\text{th}}$

Assuming $S_{\text{th}}(\Delta \omega)$ is the standard **one-sided** thermal noise power spectral density (in $\text{V}^2/\text{Hz}$) at $V_{\text{out}}$, we can compute the single-sideband (SSB) phase noise $\mathcal{L}(\Delta \omega)$ via narrowband FM (or equivalently, linear phase-domain analysis):

#### Method A: Narrowband FM Representation
1. **Model noise in a $1\text{-Hz}$ bandwidth:** Within a $1\text{-Hz}$ bandwidth centered at offset $\Delta \omega$, the mean-square noise voltage at $V_{\text{out}}$ is $\overline{v_n^2} = S_{\text{th}}(\Delta \omega) \cdot (1\text{ Hz})$. Representing this narrowband component as a sinusoid $v_n(t) = V_p \cos(\Delta \omega \, t)$ with average power $\frac{V_p^2}{2} = S_{\text{th}}(\Delta \omega)$ gives:
   $$V_p = \sqrt{2 S_{\text{th}}(\Delta \omega)}$$

2. **Integrate frequency to find excess phase:**
   $$\Delta \omega_{\text{osc}}(t) = K_{\text{sup}} V_p \cos(\Delta \omega \, t) \implies \phi(t) = \int \Delta \omega_{\text{osc}}(t) \, dt = \frac{K_{\text{sup}} V_p}{\Delta \omega} \sin(\Delta \omega \, t)$$

3. **Evaluate sideband-to-carrier power ratio:** For small phase deviations ($\left|\frac{K_{\text{sup}} V_p}{\Delta \omega}\right| \ll 1$), the differential VCO output $V_{\text{osc}}(t) = V_0 \cos[\omega_0 t + \phi(t)]$ expands as:
   $$V_{\text{osc}}(t) \approx V_0 \cos(\omega_0 t) - \frac{V_0 K_{\text{sup}} V_p}{2 \Delta \omega} \cos[(\omega_0 - \Delta \omega)t] + \frac{V_0 K_{\text{sup}} V_p}{2 \Delta \omega} \cos[(\omega_0 + \Delta \omega)t]$$
   Dividing the power of one sideband, $P_{\text{USB}} = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{V_0 K_{\text{sup}} V_p}{2\Delta \omega}\right)^2$, by the carrier power, $P_{\text{carrier}} = \frac{V_0^2}{2}$, and substituting $V_p^2 = 2 S_{\text{th}}(\Delta \omega)$ yields:
   $$\mathcal{L}(\Delta \omega) = \frac{P_{\text{USB}}}{P_{\text{carrier}}} = \frac{K_{\text{sup}}^2 V_p^2}{4 \Delta \omega^2} = \frac{K_{\text{sup}}^2 \, S_{\text{th}}(\Delta \omega)}{2 \, \Delta \omega^2}$$

#### Method B: Phase-Domain Transfer Function
Because phase is the integral of frequency ($\Phi(s) = \frac{K_{\text{sup}}}{s} V_{\text{out}}(s)$), the one-sided excess-phase PSD is:
$$S_{\phi}(\Delta \omega) = \left|\frac{K_{\text{sup}}}{j \Delta \omega}\right|^2 S_{\text{th}}(\Delta \omega) = \frac{K_{\text{sup}}^2}{\Delta \omega^2} S_{\text{th}}(\Delta \omega)$$
Upconversion around the carrier splits the phase power equally between the upper and lower sidebands, giving the standard relation $\mathcal{L}(\Delta \omega) = \frac{1}{2} S_{\phi}(\Delta \omega)$.

---

### 3. Summary Formula

Using $|K_{\text{sup}}| \approx K_{\text{VCO}}$, the VCO output phase noise at offset $\Delta \omega = 2\pi \Delta f$ is:

$$\mathcal{L}(\Delta \omega) \approx \frac{K_{\text{VCO}}^2 \, S_{\text{th}}(\Delta \omega)}{2 \, \Delta \omega^2} = \frac{K_{\text{VCO},f}^2 \, S_{\text{th}}(\Delta f)}{2 \, \Delta f^2}$$

> * **Around $\omega_0$:** Because $V_{\text{out}}$ drives the center tap of a symmetric differential VCO, common-mode LDO noise near $\omega_0$ does not excite the differential tank mode (absent layout/device mismatch).
